title: The Universal Machine: from Maida Vale to Wilmslow by way of Hut 8
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Warrington Lodge, Maida Vale: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Alan Turing'; English Heritage blue plaque). Coordinate corrected: the incoming pool carried two different pins for this one doorway, 51.5228/-0.1859 in the geography lens and 51.5262/-0.1859 in the afterlife lens, both wrong; Wikipedia ('Colonnade Hotel') puts 2 Warrington Crescent at 51.5243, -0.1846.
stops.campa: In a private nursing home on Warrington Crescent a son is born to Ethel Turing while her husband Julius is home on leave from the Indian Civil Service. The house is trading as the Warrington Lodge Medical and Surgery Home for Ladies; it will be a hotel by 1935, and a blue plaque will go up on its front in 1998. The parents return to Madras within the year. The child and his elder brother John stay behind in England, boarded with strangers, and that arrangement holds for most of a childhood.
suggested_refs: 2 Warrington Crescent, Maida Vale, with the English Heritage plaque unveiled by Andrew Hodges on 23 June 1998
sources: English Heritage blue plaque, 2 Warrington Crescent

stops.name: Baston Lodge, St Leonards-on-Sea: the Wards' house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Hodges gives the boarding arrangement for roughly 1913-1926 without a start date; the day and month default to 01. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 50.8546/0.568, about 1.1 km too far east, to the Upper Maze Hill geocode. St Michael's School, 20 Charles Road, is folded into this stop; its own corrected pin is 50.8560, 0.5564.
stops.campa: At Baston Lodge on Upper Maze Hill a retired army couple, Colonel and Mrs Ward, take in the two Turing boys through the school holidays while their parents cross back and forth to India. The household runs on regimental time. Alan is enrolled at St Michael's, a small day school on Charles Road, where the headmistress notices that the boy's arithmetic runs ahead of anything she can set him. Julius and Ethel come back from Madras on leave and go out again. The boys' address stays the Wards'.
suggested_refs: Baston Lodge, Upper Maze Hill, St Leonards-on-Sea, with its later plaque
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Frant: the preparatory school at Hazelhurst
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years 1922-1926 (Wikipedia), month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 51.087/0.307 sits 2.8 km southeast of the village, and 'Hazelhurst, Frant' returns no OpenStreetMap match at all, so the school building is not independently locatable. The pin is the village of Frant, East Sussex. The pool's chronology lens says 'Sussex', its geography lens 'East Sussex'.
stops.campa: He boards at Hazelhurst near Frant, a preparatory school built around Latin and Greek, and his enthusiasms run the other way: chemistry, arithmetic, the behaviour of things. Masters who prize a classical polish find him untidy and single-minded. He is nine when he arrives and thirteen when he leaves for Sherborne. In those four years nothing remarkable is recorded of him beyond an odd persistence at problems nobody has set him, and a handwriting his teachers describe as the worst they have seen.
suggested_refs: The village of Frant, East Sussex; the Hazelhurst school buildings are not locatable in any reachable source
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Southampton: the ride through the General Strike
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The ride is a widely repeated anecdote from Hodges; the route and the inn are documented nowhere reachable. The day is inferred from the General Strike, 3 to 12 May 1926, and is not attested.
stops.campa: The General Strike stops the trains in the first week of May, and the boy due to start at Sherborne does not wait for them to run again. He rides a bicycle some sixty miles from Southampton into Dorset alone, stopping overnight at an inn on the way, and reports for the first day of term on time. He is thirteen and has never seen the school. Neither the route nor the name of the inn was ever written down, and Hodges, who carries the story, gives no source for either.
suggested_refs: The Southampton to Sherborne road, ridden alone in the first week of the 1926 General Strike
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Westcott House, Sherborne School: five years at odds
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1926-1931 (Wikipedia; Hodges); the arrival day is inferred from the strike ride. The quotation is carried as reconstruction: the pool saw the headmaster's report only through a page summary of turing.org.uk, not a raw archival scan, and it is a line about Turing, not by him.
stops.campa: He boards in Westcott House and spends five years at odds with the place. Sherborne teaches classics and games; Turing does chemistry in his study, reads Einstein on his own account, and returns marks that alarm his housemasters in every subject that is not mathematics. His headmaster writes home that a boy who means to be solely a scientific specialist is wasting his time at a public school. He stays the course, and leaves in 1931 with a scholarship in mathematics to King's College, Cambridge.
stops.quote: If he is to be solely a Scientific Specialist, he is wasting his time at a Public School.
stops.quote_source: Sherborne School headmaster's report on Alan Turing, quoted in Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma, via turing.org.uk
suggested_refs: Westcott House, Sherborne School, Dorset
The surviving school reports on Turing in the Sherborne archive
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Sherborne: the death of Christopher Morcom
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1930 (turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry); the day is not given in the verified pool and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Christopher Morcom is a year above him, quicker at astronomy, and the only person at Sherborne who meets him at his own level. For two years they trade problems and observations across the gap between their houses. In February 1930 Morcom dies of complications of bovine tuberculosis contracted from milk drunk years before, and Turing writes to his mother about him for years afterwards. He turns from that death to the question of whether mind can survive matter, and then to the question of what a mind is doing when it computes.
stops.quote: I do not think that this argument is sufficiently substantial to require refutation. Consolation would be more appropriate: perhaps this should be sought in the transmigration of souls.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (1950), section 6, reply to the Heads in the Sand Objection, p. 444, written twenty years after Morcom's death
suggested_refs: Turing's letters to Frances Isobel Morcom, Christopher's mother, in the King's College archive
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry
Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

segments.name: King's College, and the Universal Machine

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: the undergraduate
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1931-1934 (Wikipedia; King's College archives); the day defaults to 01. The Trinity scholarship failure of December 1929 is attested by Hodges and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin at 52.2054, 0.1163.
stops.campa: He goes up to King's in February 1931, having failed the previous December to win a scholarship at Trinity, and takes first-class honours in mathematics in 1934. Cambridge is where he hears Max Newman lecture on the Entscheidungsproblem, Hilbert's question whether a mechanical procedure exists that can decide the truth of any mathematical statement. Turing will answer it in a language nobody expects, by building the mechanical procedure first. That summer he is photographed on Sark, in the Channel Islands, in a swimming costume.
suggested_refs: King's College, Cambridge
The 1931 Sark photographs in the turing.org.uk Internet Scrapbook
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: elected Fellow at twenty-two
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1935 (Wikipedia); the pool gives the year only, so month and day default to 01. The Smith's Prize of 1936 (turing.org.uk, DNB) is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: At twenty-two he is elected a Fellow of King's on a dissertation proving a version of the central limit theorem, which he has worked out from nothing without knowing that Lindeberg established it eleven years earlier. The college elects him regardless. The following year he takes the Smith's Prize for work on probability. He has rooms, a stipend, no teaching he cannot avoid, and the whole of 1935 and 1936 to spend on a question about what a machine can and cannot be made to do.
suggested_refs: Turing's 1935 fellowship dissertation, 'On the Gaussian Error Function', King's College archive
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Cambridge: On Computable Numbers
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool carried 1936-08, which matches nothing. Wikipedia's sequence: submitted 28 May 1936, read to the London Mathematical Society 12 November 1936, printed in Proc. LMS ser. 2 vol. 42 in two parts on 30 November and 23 December 1936, with a Correction in vol. 43 (1938) after Bernays found errors. This stop is dated to the submission.
stops.campa: He writes a paper that defines a machine: a tape, a head that reads and writes one symbol at a time, a finite table of instructions. From it he builds a universal machine, one that takes the description of any other machine and does what that machine does. Then he shows that no such machine can decide in general whether an arbitrary machine will ever halt, and the Entscheidungsproblem is answered in the negative. He is twenty-four. Alonzo Church at Princeton has reached the same result by another road, months earlier.
stops.quote: The "computable" numbers may be described briefly as the real numbers whose expressions as a decimal are calculable by finite means.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem', Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, series 2, vol. 42 (1936), p. 230, opening sentence
suggested_refs: The printed Proc. LMS ser. 2 vol. 42 offprint, with the 1938 Correction in vol. 43
sources: Alan Turing, 'On Computable Numbers' (1936), verified against PDF text

stops.name: Fine Hall, Princeton: the corridor of the Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1936 to July 1938 (Wikipedia); the day defaults to 01. Coordinate corrected and inherited: the pool's 40.343/-74.6551 matches neither the Fine Hall of the 1930s (today's Jones Hall) nor the 1970 tower. This pin is taken byte-identical from dirac.journey.json and einstein.journey.json.
stops.campa: He crosses to Princeton to work under Alonzo Church, whose lambda calculus answered the Entscheidungsproblem first. Fine Hall houses the university mathematicians and the Institute for Advanced Study at once, since the Institute has no building of its own until 1939, so one corridor holds John von Neumann, Albert Einstein and Hermann Weyl together; Paul Dirac had worked in the same building two years before. Turing keeps to himself, and builds a binary multiplier in the physics workshop, cutting and winding the relays with his own hands.
suggested_refs: Fine Hall, Princeton (now Jones Hall), which housed both the mathematics department and the Institute for Advanced Study until 1939

stops.name: Princeton: the doctorate on ordinal logics
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1938 (Wikipedia; Princeton graduate records); the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: His thesis, Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals, takes the incompleteness he proved in 1936 and asks what happens if the missing truths are added back as axioms, transfinitely, ordinal after ordinal. The answer is that the adding never finishes. On the way the work introduces the oracle machine, a computing machine granted answers to questions it cannot compute for itself. Church signs the degree in June 1938. It is the least read of Turing's major papers and the one von Neumann reads closest.
suggested_refs: Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals, Princeton PhD dissertation, 1938

stops.name: The Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton: the post declined
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. john_von_neumann.journey.json establishes his Princeton chair from 1933 and cites Dyson's Turing's Cathedral elsewhere, but the offer to Turing is not stated in that file; it is carried from outside knowledge. Month and day are placed at the end of the Princeton residence. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from john_von_neumann.journey.json, robert_oppenheimer.journey.json and claude_shannon.journey.json.
stops.campa: John von Neumann, one of the six founding professors of the Institute in 1933, offers Turing a post at the end of his doctorate. Turing declines it and sails for England. The Institute has no ground of its own yet: Fuld Hall opens only the following year, and the pin here marks a lawn. Robert Oppenheimer will direct the place from 1947, and Claude Shannon will spend a fellowship year in it in 1940. Turing goes back to King's, and to the Government Code and Cypher School, which has already asked for him.
suggested_refs: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study, opened 1939, a year after Turing left Princeton

stops.name: 54 Broadway, Westminster: the Code and Cypher School
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1938 (Wikipedia; Hodges); the day defaults to 01. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 51.4996/-0.131, about 215 m east of the site, to the Nominatim geocode for 54/55 Broadway SW1H. Marian Rejewski, whose work the last sentence describes, is queued in the atlas but not yet researched.
stops.campa: The Government Code and Cypher School keeps offices at Broadway Buildings, opposite St James's Park station, behind a brass plate naming a company that does not exist. Turing works there part time from September 1938, trained by Dilly Knox on the commercial Enigma, while still drawing his fellowship at King's. Poland's Cipher Bureau has already broken the military machine, and in July 1939 hands the British its methods and a reconstructed Enigma at Pyry outside Warsaw. Turing inherits a solved problem that is about to become unsolvable again.
suggested_refs: Broadway Buildings, 54 Broadway, Westminster, headquarters of GC&CS until 1939
The Pyry conference, July 1939, where the Polish Cipher Bureau handed over its methods
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: The stable yard cottage, Bletchley Park: the day after the declaration
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; Bletchley Park Trust).
stops.campa: Britain declares war on the third of September 1939. Turing reports to Bletchley Park on the fourth and is put in the cottage in the mansion's stable yard, alongside Dilly Knox's small team. The German navy has changed its indicator system and the Polish methods no longer reach the traffic. Within three months Turing has the naval indicator out and has invented Banburismus, a sequential procedure worked with punched sheets and a running estimate of the odds, which cuts the number of Enigma settings a machine has to test before the day's traffic goes stale.
suggested_refs: The cottages in the stable yard at Bletchley Park, where Knox's team worked in 1939

stops.name: Hut 8, Bletchley Park: the naval traffic
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1939 for the indicator solution and Banburismus (Wikipedia); the day defaults to 01. Turing headed Hut 8 from 1939 to 1942 (Bletchley Park Trust).
stops.campa: Hut 8 is Turing's section and the German naval Enigma is its problem: the traffic that directs the U-boat packs across the Atlantic convoy routes. The hut works by crib, by Banburismus, by material seized from weather trawlers and from sinking submarines, and by machine. What comes out of it is passed to the Admiralty's tracking room dressed as the product of agents or direction finding, because the fact that Enigma is broken is worth more than any single convoy that could be saved by admitting it.
suggested_refs: Hut 8, Bletchley Park, restored to its wartime state by the Bletchley Park Trust

stops.name: The British Tabulating Machine Company, Letchworth: where the bombes are built
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1939-1940 (Wikipedia, 'Bombe'; Bletchley Park Trust); the month and day are not given in the pool and default to 01.
stops.campa: The bombe is engineered and built at the British Tabulating Machine Company works on Icknield Way in Letchworth, under chief engineer Harold Keen, from Turing's design. It is a machine for testing an assumption at speed: a rack of turning drums that runs a guessed crib through Enigma's wirings and stops the instant the assumption contradicts itself. Letchworth builds them all through the war, and the Wrens who will run them at Bletchley and its outstations are trained on the machines here before the machines leave.
suggested_refs: The British Tabulating Machine Company works, Icknield Way, Letchworth
Harold Keen's engineering drawings for the bombe

stops.name: Bletchley Park: the bombe named Victory
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Bombe'). Attribution corrected: the pool credited this first machine to Turing's design 'with Gordon Welchman's improvements', but Victory specifically lacked Welchman's diagonal board. The first machine fitted with it was Agnus Dei, installed 8 August 1940. Bletchley coordinate inherited byte-identical from ian_fleming.journey.json.
stops.campa: The first bombe, named Victory, is installed in Hut 1 on the eighteenth of March 1940. It is built to Turing's design alone and it is slow, because it has no diagonal board; Gordon Welchman is at that moment working out what a diagonal board would do. The second machine, Agnus Dei, arrives on the eighth of August with the board fitted and does the work of many of the first kind. By the end of the war more than two hundred bombes are running at Bletchley and its outstations, and every one of them stops on a contradiction Turing worked out in 1939.
suggested_refs: The working bombe rebuild at Bletchley Park, completed 2007

stops.name: Bletchley Park: Operation Ruthless cancelled
stops.date_confidence: attested via ian_fleming.journey.json, stop on Operation Ruthless. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from that file.
stops.campa: Ian Fleming, personal assistant to the Director of Naval Intelligence, proposes Operation Ruthless: ditch a captured German bomber in the Channel with a crew in Luftwaffe uniform, wait for the German rescue boat, kill its crew, take the boat and the Enigma material aboard it. No rescue boat appears where it is wanted and the operation is cancelled. Turing and Peter Twinn come to Frank Birch at Bletchley about the cancellation, and Birch writes down how they looked to him.
stops.quote: like undertakers cheated of a corpse
stops.quote_source: Frank Birch on Turing and Peter Twinn after the cancellation of Operation Ruthless, September 1940, as carried in ian_fleming.journey.json
suggested_refs: Fleming's memorandum proposing Operation Ruthless, September 1940

stops.name: Hut 8, Bletchley Park: the engagement to Joan Clarke
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1941 in Hut 8 (Wikipedia, 'Alan Turing'), month and day defaulted within that season. The incoming pool tagged this a reconstruction on the grounds that Wikipedia and turing.org.uk conflict over a Bletchley or a Manchester setting; on re-reading, the DNB entry does not contradict the Bletchley setting and no genuine conflict exists. The pool's hedge is recorded here rather than deleted.
stops.campa: Joan Clarke is the only woman doing cryptanalytic work in Hut 8, and she is graded and paid as a linguist because the establishment has no other category to put her in. In the spring of 1941 Turing proposes marriage and she accepts. Within days he tells her he has homosexual tendencies, and she is not put off. He breaks the engagement himself that summer. They go on working side by side at the same problem in the same hut, and she remains his friend until his death thirteen years later.
suggested_refs: Joan Clarke's own later accounts of Hut 8 and of the engagement
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Bletchley Park: the letter to Churchill
stops.date_confidence: attested for the letter (Wikipedia). Churchill's 'Action this day' minute in reply is standard in the literature but is not in the verified pool for this journey, and is carried here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Turing, Hugh Alexander, Gordon Welchman and Stuart Milner-Barry write directly to the Prime Minister, over the heads of their own service chiefs, to say that Bletchley Park is short of typists, clerks and machines, and that breaks are being lost for want of them. Milner-Barry carries the letter to Downing Street by hand. Churchill minutes it the same day: action this day, make sure they have all they want on extreme priority, and report to me that this has been done. The staff are found within weeks.
suggested_refs: The 28 October 1941 letter to Churchill, held at the National Archives

stops.name: Bletchley Park: Turingery and the Lorenz machine
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1942 (Wikipedia); the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The Lorenz machine carries the traffic between the German high command and its army groups, and Bletchley has never seen one. From intercepted teleprinter tape alone the section reconstructs its logical structure, and in July 1942 Turing supplies a hand method, called Turingery in the huts, for recovering the wheel patterns that change with every key period. It is done with paper and pencil. What it opens will later be worked by Colossus, the first large electronic digital machine, which Turing does not design.
suggested_refs: The Colossus rebuild at The National Museum of Computing, Bletchley Park

stops.name: The Navy Department, Washington: the American bombes
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is attested to November 1942 (Wikipedia; turing.org.uk); the day defaults to 01. Venue corrected: the pool pinned the Naval Communications Annex on Nebraska Avenue, but the Navy only took over that site by the end of 1942 and bought the land on 20 July 1943, so in November 1942 OP-20-G was still in the Main Navy Building on Constitution Avenue. The coordinate used here is that building's site and is a reconstruction, not a value any pool source supplied.
stops.campa: Turing sails for the United States in November 1942 and works in Washington with the American navy's cryptanalysts on naval Enigma and on their bombe programme, which is being built to a heavier and different design from his own. He is admitted to the work only after an argument at the top, because the Americans have not yet decided how much they will be told or shown. The codebreakers are still in the Main Navy Building on Constitution Avenue at this date; the Nebraska Avenue site they will be famous for is not theirs yet.
suggested_refs: The Main Navy and Munitions Buildings on Constitution Avenue, home of OP-20-G until 1943
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: National Cash Register, Building 26, Dayton: the four-wheel machines
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1942 (Wikipedia, 'United States Naval Computing Machine Laboratory'), which is also the correction to the pool's chronology entry folding Dayton into the November crossing. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 39.7589/-84.1916 is the Dayton city centroid, 2.9 km north of Building 26 at Patterson Boulevard and Stewart Street.
stops.campa: In Building 26 of the National Cash Register plant, at Patterson Boulevard and Stewart Street, the United States Naval Computing Machine Laboratory is building high-speed bombes against the four-wheel naval Enigma. Turing inspects the work in December 1942 and writes a report on the design, not all of it admiring. The American machines, when they run, are faster than Letchworth's and there are more of them, and the two navies divide the naval traffic between them. The Art Deco building comes down in January 2008.
suggested_refs: NCR Building 26, Dayton, Ohio, demolished January 2008
Turing's 1942 report on the American bombe design
sources: Wikipedia, 'United States Naval Computing Machine Laboratory'
Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Bell Telephone Laboratories, West Street: tea with Claude Shannon
stops.date_confidence: attested via claude_shannon.journey.json, stop 'The Bell Labs cafeteria, tea with Turing', which dates the visit to about two months in early 1943 and names Turing explicitly. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from that file; the geography lens of this journey's own pool gave 40.7367, -74.0086 for the same building, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than averaged.
stops.campa: For about two months at the start of 1943 Turing works at Bell Telephone Laboratories on West Street, on the mathematics of enciphering speech for the transatlantic line between Roosevelt and Churchill. Claude Shannon is in the same building on the same problem, and the two take tea together most days, forbidden by their own governments to discuss the work either is actually doing. So they discuss machines instead. Turing gives Shannon On Computable Numbers; Shannon tells Turing what he thinks a machine could be brought to do.
suggested_refs: Bell Telephone Laboratories, 463 West Street, Manhattan
The SIGSALY secure voice terminal, Bell Labs, 1943
sources: claude_shannon.journey.json, stop 'The Bell Labs cafeteria, tea with Turing'
Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Hanslope Park: Delilah, and the hut handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1944-1945 (Wikipedia; Hodges); month and day default to 01. The return to Bletchley in March 1943 and Hugh Alexander's formal succession at Hut 8 are attested to that month (Wikipedia) and are folded into this stop. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 52.0733/-0.8004 to Wikipedia's value for Hanslope Park, a shift of 3.6 km.
stops.campa: Turing comes home in March 1943, and Hugh Alexander formally takes the head of Hut 8, a post Turing had in practice already left. He moves to the Radio Security Service station at Hanslope Park, an army camp behind wire, and builds Delilah there with a young engineer named Donald Bayley: a portable speech scrambler, small enough to carry, which works and which nobody orders. He lives on the site. The war ends with Delilah demonstrated on a recording of a Churchill speech, and then shelved.
suggested_refs: Hanslope Park, Buckinghamshire, requisitioned 1941 for the Radio Security Service
The Delilah speech scrambler, built 1944-1945 with Donald Bayley
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: 78 High Street, Hampton: the medal that cannot be explained
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1945-1947 (Wikipedia); month and day default to 01. The OBE, attested to 1946 with an unpublished citation (Wikipedia; turing.org.uk), is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: He lodges at 78 High Street in Hampton and commutes to Teddington. He is thirty-three, out of the secret world and forbidden to say a word about what he did inside it, and he is appointed OBE in 1946 for services the citation declines to describe. The war work will stay classified for another thirty years. Fewer than a dozen people alive know what a room of purpose-built machines can be made to do to a problem at speed. He is one of them. The engineers he now works beside at Teddington have not been told, and will not be.
suggested_refs: 78 High Street, Hampton, with its later plaque
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Bushy House, National Physical Laboratory: the ACE report
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia). Coordinate corrected from the pool's 51.4257/-0.34, which is the NPL site pin about 590 m north of Bushy House itself.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of February 1946 Turing reads a paper to the executive committee of the National Physical Laboratory setting out the Automatic Computing Engine: a complete design for a stored-program electronic computer, with costings, circuit details and sample programs written out. It is more detailed than anything else in existence and faster in conception than what Britain is building. Charles Babbage drew engines a century earlier that were never cut in metal. Turing's design is buildable, and the NPL does not build it.
suggested_refs: Bushy House, National Physical Laboratory, Teddington
Turing's 1946 ACE report to the NPL executive committee

stops.name: Loughborough: the marathon championship
stops.date_confidence: contested, and not resolved. The pool gave August 1949 at Windsor, which is wrong twice: it conflates the AAA championship with the Polytechnic Marathon, which alone ran the Windsor to Chiswick course, and Wikipedia rules out 1949 by framing the run as a tryout for the 1948 British Olympic team, only 11 minutes off Thomas Richards' 1948 silver-medal time. The standard secondary account gives August 1947 at Loughborough, fifth in 2:46:03, and is used here. No primary results archive was reachable: arrs.run returned HTTP 512 and no Wikipedia article on the AAA Marathon exists, so the Loughborough venue rests on secondary accounts alone. His Walton Athletic Club membership, folded into this stop, is not in dispute.
stops.campa: Frustrated by the pace of the engineering at Teddington, Turing runs. He joins Walton Athletic Club, trains alone over long distances on the roads, and in the Amateur Athletic Association marathon championship finishes fifth in two hours forty-six minutes and three seconds, within eleven minutes of the time that will take the Olympic silver medal the following year. A club official calls him one of the best runners in the country. An injury ends the Olympic prospect. He keeps running to the end of his life.
suggested_refs: Walton Athletic Club records of Turing's membership and training
The 1947 AAA Marathon Championship results
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Bushy House, Teddington: the Pilot ACE runs
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1950 (Wikipedia); the day is not given in the pool and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: The Pilot ACE, a reduced version of Turing's design built by the engineers who stayed at the NPL after he left, executes its first program in May 1950. It runs useful commercial and scientific work for years, and its architecture goes on into the English Electric DEUCE. By then Turing has been in Manchester two years. He is not at Teddington for the first run, and the full Automatic Computing Engine he designed in 1946 is never built anywhere to his specification.
suggested_refs: The Pilot ACE, preserved at the Science Museum, London

stops.name: The Computing Machine Laboratory, Manchester: the Baby runs a stored program
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1948 (turing.org.uk, DNB). The precise date of 21 June 1948, and the seventeen-instruction highest-factor program, are the standard account and lie outside the verified pool, which gives the month only. Note the order: the machine runs before Turing arrives in Manchester in October.
stops.campa: In the Computing Machine Laboratory at Manchester, Freddie Williams and Tom Kilburn build a small machine to test a cathode ray tube memory, and it runs a program held in its own store: seventeen instructions searching for the highest factor of a number, fifty-two minutes of computation. It is the first time a machine executes a program written into its own memory rather than plugged or punched into it. Turing is not in Manchester yet. Max Newman, who lectured him at Cambridge on the Entscheidungsproblem, has brought the project here.
stops.quote: In attempting to construct such machines we should not be irreverently usurping His power of creating souls, any more than we are in the procreation of children: rather we are, in either case, instruments of His will providing mansions for the souls that He creates.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (1950), section 6, reply to the Theological Objection, p. 443
suggested_refs: The Small-Scale Experimental Machine replica at the Science and Industry Museum, Manchester
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: The University of Manchester: deputy director
stops.date_confidence: contested, not resolved. turing.org.uk (DNB) gives October 1948 for the move as deputy director of the Computing Machine Laboratory; Wikipedia gives a 1948 reader appointment and 1949 for the deputy directorship. Both are recorded. The day defaults to 01. Turochamp, attested to 1948-1950 (Wikipedia), is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Turing arrives in October 1948 as reader in mathematics and deputy director of the Computing Machine Laboratory, a title over a job with no fixed duties, since Williams and Kilburn build the hardware and guard it. He writes the programmer's handbook for the Manchester Mark 1 in a base thirty-two notation of his own devising that other people find close to unusable. With the economist David Champernowne he works out Turochamp, a chess program on paper, because no machine exists yet that can be made to run it.
stops.quote: Machines take me by surprise with great frequency.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (1950), section 6, reply to Lady Lovelace's Objection, p. 450
suggested_refs: Turing's Programmers' Handbook for the Manchester Electronic Computer
The Turochamp algorithm, played out by hand in 1952
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Manchester: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1950, Mind new series vol. LIX no. 236, pp. 433-460 (verified against PDF text); the day defaults to 01. Place corrected: the pool attached this quotation to the National Physical Laboratory, Teddington, but Turing had left the NPL in 1948 and was at Manchester when the paper was written and published. The widely circulated reprint's header reading 'Mind 49' is an error of the reprint.
stops.campa: He publishes Computing Machinery and Intelligence in the philosophical journal Mind, and opens by refusing the question he has asked. Instead of defining thought he describes a game: an interrogator in one room, a machine and a person in another, a teletype between them. If the interrogator cannot tell which is which, the question has been answered as well as it can be answered. He then takes nine objections in turn, among them Ada Lovelace's, that a machine can originate nothing, and answers each one on its own ground.
stops.quote: I propose to consider the question, "Can machines think?"
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (October 1950), opening sentence of section 1, p. 433
suggested_refs: Mind LIX/236, October 1950, pp. 433-460
Ada Lovelace's Note G of 1843, the source of Lady Lovelace's Objection
sources: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950), verified against PDF text

stops.name: The Royal Society, London: elected on a fifteen-year-old paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1951 (Wikipedia; turing.org.uk); the pool gives the year only, so month and day default to 01. The pin is the Society's house at Carlton House Terrace. The BBC radio talk on machine intelligence, also attested to 1951 with no date (Britannica), is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects Turing a Fellow on a citation resting chiefly on the 1936 paper on computable numbers, written when he was twenty-four and now fifteen years behind him. The war work cannot be cited, because officially it does not exist. Max Newman, who proposed him, and Bertrand Russell are among the few who know what the 1936 paper did and what the man who wrote it did afterwards. In the same year he broadcasts on the BBC on whether a machine can be said to think, and argues that it can.
stops.quote: I believe that in about fifty years' time it will be possible to programme computers, with a storage capacity of about 10^9, to make them play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator will not have more than 70 per cent. chance of making the right identification after five minutes of questioning.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (1950), section 6, p. 442
suggested_refs: The Royal Society, 6-9 Carlton House Terrace, London
Turing's 1951 BBC radio talk on machine intelligence
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Manchester: The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The pool gave 1952-01, which is supported by nothing: the paper appeared in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, vol. 237, no. 641, pp. 37-72, in the issue dated 14 August 1952 (DOI 10.1098/rstb.1952.0012). turing.org.uk gives November 1951 as the submission date, the likeliest source of the early-1952 drift. That the numerical work was run on the Ferranti Mark 1 is standard in the literature but not in the verified pool.
stops.campa: Turing turns the Manchester machine on biology. The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis shows that two chemicals diffusing and reacting through a uniform sheet of tissue will not stay uniform: small fluctuations grow into stable patterns of spots and stripes out of nothing but diffusion rates and rate constants. He is proposing a mechanism by which an undifferentiated egg becomes a striped animal, with no plan anywhere in it. He runs the numerical work on the machine itself, which almost nobody is yet doing in biology.
stops.quote: The nervous system is certainly not a discrete-state machine.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (1950), section 6, Argument from Continuity in the Nervous System, p. 451
suggested_refs: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, vol. 237, no. 641 (14 August 1952), pp. 37-72
The Ferranti Mark 1 at Manchester, on which the morphogenesis calculations were run
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Hollymeade, 43 Adlington Road, Wilmslow: the burglary reported
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia). Two corrections to the pool: the house was called Hollymeade, not 'Copper Folly' (Wikipedia, 'Legacy of Alan Turing', on the plaque unveiled there 7 June 2004), and the coordinate 53.3251/-2.2367 is essentially the Wilmslow town centroid, 2.2 to 3.0 km west of Adlington Road. The pool also conflated arrest with conviction: the charge is February 1952, the trial 31 March.
stops.campa: Turing buys a house called Hollymeade on Adlington Road in Wilmslow, seven miles from the university, and lives in it alone. In January 1952 he begins a relationship with Arnold Murray, nineteen years old, met on Oxford Road in Manchester. On the twenty-third the house is burgled by an acquaintance of Murray's. Turing reports the burglary to the police and, in the course of their investigation, tells them without evasion what his relationship with Murray is. Both men are charged in February with gross indecency.
suggested_refs: Hollymeade, 43 Adlington Road, Wilmslow, with the plaque unveiled 7 June 2004
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Wilmslow: the letter to Norman Routledge
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1952, between the charge and the guilty plea; original in the Turing Archive, King's College, Cambridge, quoted in this form by Hodges in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, section 9, citing the archive. The day defaults to 01. The pool carried a misquoted variant beginning 'I'm rather afraid' and tagged it a reconstruction; the corrected wording is used, but no archival image of the manuscript was fetched, so the upgrade rests on the SEP's citation rather than on the archive itself.
stops.campa: Between the charge and the trial Turing writes to Norman Routledge, a former student at King's, telling him what has happened and what he expects will follow from it. The letter is unhurried. Halfway down he sets out a syllogism, in the form he has spent his working life studying: premises that are each of them true, a conclusion that does not follow from them, and a world entirely prepared to draw it anyway. He signs the letter yours in distress, Alan. It is now in the archive at King's.
stops.quote: I'm afraid that the following syllogism may be used by some in the future / Turing believes machines think / Turing lies with men / Therefore machines do not think
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing to Norman Routledge, February 1952, Turing Archive, King's College, Cambridge; quoted in Andrew Hodges, 'Alan Turing', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, section 9, and in Alan Turing: The Enigma
suggested_refs: The Routledge letter, Turing Archive, King's College, Cambridge
sources: Andrew Hodges, 'Alan Turing', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, section 9
Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Knutsford Quarter Sessions: the conviction
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; Hodges). This is the date of trial and conviction, which the pool's chronology entry mislabelled as the arrest.
stops.campa: He is tried at Knutsford Quarter Sessions on the thirty-first of March and pleads guilty rather than contest the charge, under the same 1885 statute that convicted Oscar Wilde. He is not sent to prison. What he accepts instead is a year's probation on condition of hormone treatment: synthetic oestrogen, by injection and then by implant, for twelve months, which makes him impotent and grows breast tissue. The university keeps him on and he goes on working. What he loses is his security clearance, and with it the cryptanalytic consultancy.
suggested_refs: Knutsford Quarter Sessions, Cheshire
The Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885, section 11, under which he was charged
sources: turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry
Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Bergen: the journey to Norway
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Hodges places the Norwegian journey in the summer after the conviction; the itinerary and any specific Bergen locations are not independently documented, and the month and day are placed within that summer. The further security scare at the Wilmslow house, folded into this stop, is attested to March 1953 (turing.org.uk, DNB).
stops.campa: In the summer after the conviction Turing travels to Norway, where the law is not what English law is, and meets a young man in Bergen. His movements are noted. In March 1953 a foreign visitor to the house at Wilmslow brings the police and Special Branch back to his door, and the file on him is not closed afterwards. The security service knows what he did in Hut 8. It has no procedure for a man who holds that and a conviction at once, and it keeps his file open instead.
suggested_refs: Bergen, Norway, summer 1952
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma
turing.org.uk, Dictionary of National Biography entry

stops.name: Hollymeade, Wilmslow: the apple beside the bed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 7 June 1954 by the chronology and afterlife lenses (Wikipedia); the geography lens says he was found on 8 June, a day after taking cyanide, which is consistent with a death on the 7th but is never reconciled in the pool. The cause is contested and is left contested: the inquest returned suicide, his mother maintained accidental poisoning from his home electroplating work, and the apple was never tested for cyanide, which is the crux.
stops.campa: On the evening of the seventh of June 1954 Turing takes cyanide at Hollymeade. His housekeeper finds him the next morning with a half-eaten apple beside the bed. The apple is never tested. The inquest returns a verdict of suicide. His mother Sara insists to the end of her life that he was careless with chemicals in the little laboratory in his spare room, where he electroplated spoons with potassium cyanide, and that it was an accident. He is forty-one, and the two accounts have never been reconciled.
suggested_refs: The inquest record, Cheshire, June 1954
Sara Turing's memoir of her son, published 1959
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Woking Crematorium: no grave and no stone
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Woking Crematorium'; Hodges). Coordinate corrected and reconciled: the pool carried three different values for one crematorium, 51.3273/-0.5804 in the geography lens and 51.3168/-0.5623 in the afterlife lens, against Wikipedia's 51.3118, -0.6027 for the Hermitage Road site. That his father's ashes had been scattered there earlier could not be independently confirmed.
stops.campa: The body is cremated at Woking on the twelfth of June 1954 and the ashes are scattered in the grounds. There is no grave and no stone, and there will be none. Almost nobody attends. The wartime work stays secret for another twenty years, so nothing said over him can name what he did between 1939 and 1945; the notices in the papers describe a Manchester mathematician who had written an interesting article about whether machines could think, and give his age, and stop there.
suggested_refs: Woking Crematorium, Hermitage Road, Surrey, where the ashes were scattered without a marker
sources: Andrew Hodges, Alan Turing: The Enigma

stops.name: Sackville Gardens, Manchester: the man on the bench
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Alan Turing Memorial'): Glyn Hughes, unveiled 23 June 2001, about £15,000 raised by Richard Humphry's memorial fund, Derek Jacobi patron. Two corrections to the pool: the Enigma ciphertext is on the bronze bench, not the plinth, and the popular decoding is impossible, since Enigma cannot encipher a letter as itself and that reading shares letters with the ciphertext at matching positions. Planning documents record a different intended plaintext, 'pioneer of digital computing'. The true plaintext is unresolved.
stops.campa: A bronze figure by Glyn Hughes is unveiled in Sackville Gardens, between the university and Canal Street, on the twenty-third of June 2001, which would have been his eighty-ninth birthday. He sits on a bench holding an apple. The bench carries his name, his dates, and a line of Enigma ciphertext, IEKYF ROMSI ADXUO KVKZC GUBJ, which is popularly said to read as founder of computer science and cannot, since Enigma never enciphers a letter as itself. The plinth reads: father of computer science, mathematician, logician, wartime codebreaker, victim of prejudice.
suggested_refs: The Alan Turing Memorial, Sackville Gardens, Manchester, with its Bertrand Russell inscription

stops.name: Bletchley Park: the statue cut from slate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2007 (Wikipedia); the exact installation date is not in the verified pool and was not confirmed against Bletchley Park Trust material, so month and day default to 01. Bletchley coordinate inherited byte-identical from ian_fleming.journey.json; the afterlife lens of this pool gave 51.9975, -0.7409 for the same site.
stops.campa: At Bletchley Park, Stephen Kettle carves a life-size Turing from roughly half a million pieces of Welsh slate, commissioned by the American businessman Sidney Frank. He sits at an Enigma machine, the way the men who worked with him remembered him sitting. By the time it is installed the huts have been saved from demolition twice, the park is a museum with a queue at the door, and the work done in Hut 8 has been public knowledge for thirty years, which is longer than Turing was allowed to live after doing it.
suggested_refs: Stephen Kettle's slate statue of Turing at Bletchley Park, commissioned by Sidney Frank

stops.name: Downing Street: the apology, the pardon, the law
stops.date_confidence: attested: the apology of 10 September 2009 was issued in response to an e-petition rather than by parliamentary act (Wikipedia); the royal pardon of 24 December 2013 followed a campaign led by scientists including Stephen Hawking (Wikipedia); the Policing and Crime Act 2017 received royal assent on 31 January 2017 (UK Parliament), a date the pool could not re-verify this session. The estimate of 49,000 men is the figure carried in the pool.
stops.campa: On the tenth of September 2009, after a public petition, Prime Minister Gordon Brown issues an apology on behalf of the British government for the appalling way Turing was treated. On the twenty-fourth of December 2013 the Queen grants a posthumous pardon under the royal prerogative of mercy, an instrument used only a handful of times before. In 2017 the Policing and Crime Act extends an automatic pardon to the other men convicted under the repealed laws, some forty-nine thousand of them, nearly all dead.
suggested_refs: The 2009 e-petition and Gordon Brown's response
The Policing and Crime Act 2017, known as the Alan Turing law
sources: UK Parliament, Policing and Crime Act 2017

stops.name: The Bank of England: the face on the fifty pound note
stops.date_confidence: attested, release date confirmed by fetch of Wikipedia (Wikipedia, 'Alan Turing'). The pin is the Bank of England on Threadneedle Street. The closing quotation is verified verbatim against PDF text of Mind LIX/236, p. 460.
stops.campa: The Bank of England issues a fifty pound note carrying Turing's portrait on the twenty-third of June 2021, which would have been his hundred and ninth birthday. The design sets his signature from the Bletchley Park visitors' book beside a table from the 1936 paper on computable numbers, a technical drawing of the Automatic Computing Engine that was never built to his design, and a strip of ticker tape whose binary reads as the date of his birth. The note is legal tender in the country that prosecuted him.
stops.quote: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
stops.quote_source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind, new series vol. LIX, no. 236 (1950), final sentence, p. 460
